prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of precision.

statement.case_for: Having read the other ballots I now place the optical lattice clock (B012) ahead of my own opening first choice. Four colleagues ranked it first and two more placed it second, and the arguments converge on the same points: Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a single, clean, original concept; Ye's group took the concept to record accuracy and stability; and the result has been independently reproduced at several national metrology institutes and in intercontinental comparisons. As an instrumentalist I value that the achievement is a device whose performance is measurable and unambiguous, with downstream uses in relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the coming redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is also the most defensible attribution on the table, with no obvious third person missing within the supplied names. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize are precursors that this work builds on without duplicating.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Eriksson-Olle and Mehlig-Bernhard allude to: the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue that the full impact is still pending, and the credit story must be framed carefully against Hall and Haensch (2005), Wineland (2012) and other lattice-clock groups (ytterbium clocks, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) who are not among the credited names. Moreover, B042 is the candidate with the larger recent scientific footprint, and a field that has opened a new direction in condensed-matter physics could be argued to deserve priority over a very mature precision-measurement achievement.

responses.point: Ranks B012 only eighth, citing the pending SI redefinition and the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and single-ion clocks (Wineland) as reasons the novelty and impact may not yet be complete.
responses.response: I take the novelty point seriously but do not find it decisive. The comb and ion-clock prizes honoured the tools and the control of single quantum systems; the magic-wavelength trick that allows thousands of atoms to be interrogated while cancelling the light shift is a distinct conceptual step, and it is what moved uncertainties from 10^-16 to 10^-18. Impact does not wait on a metrological decision: the clocks are already used for geodesy and tests of constants, and international comparisons are routine. I would nevertheless accept that the citation should say what the lattice clock added, not simply refer to precision timekeeping.

responses.point: Regards Jarillo-Herrero and MacDonald as the core pair for magic-angle graphene and doubts the inclusion of Bistritzer, while ranking the lattice clock first and regarding two names as sufficient for it.
responses.response: I agree that two names suffice for B012, and I also take your point on B042: I had listed Bistritzer in my own opening as part of a natural theory-plus-experiment split, but your reading, together with the unresolved role of Cao and other experimentalists, shows the attribution there is less settled than I had assumed. That weakens my case for B042 as the first-year choice and is one reason I now put it second.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first but flags the risk of back-to-back recognition of superconducting circuits after the 2025 prize, and regards magic-angle graphene as possibly slightly early because the superconductivity mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I share both of your cautions. The 2025 prize in superconducting circuits is the reason I kept circuit QED at fourth: the physics is distinct, but I would not want the committee to follow so closely with a related award when other mature candidates are available. On twisted graphene, I agree the interpretation of the superconductivity is still being argued, and I find the lattice clock, where the claim being made is a measurable number with independent confirmation, a safer recognition of a finished achievement.

responses.point: Ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as the most unambiguous discovery, acknowledging that three-person credit for a thousands-strong collaboration is imperfect.
responses.response: I agree the discovery is beyond doubt, and as a former accelerator experimentalist I weigh it heavily. But I place it fifth precisely because of the attribution problem you name: founding spokespersons and project leaders do not capture the analysis teams or the LHC accelerator builders, and the 2013 prize already recognised the theory. Until the committee can agree what the individuals are being honoured for, I cannot support it ahead of a candidate whose credit is clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising lattice clocks.
Whether credit for other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock lineage should be acknowledged in the citation wording.
Whether the credit split in B042, including Bistritzer and Cao's role, can be settled so that it becomes the stronger candidate in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle physics) has no recorded connection to the lattice-clock, twisted-graphene or other shortlisted candidates or their credited names. I also serve as Chair, which I will handle by not favouring any field.
